links.note: Was on 32821 Getting Off the Train, the city-map activity, which has no scale in it. Calculating a real distance from a map at 2.5 cm = 500 km is the scale component, and 32823 is where the scale is defined and where the map of India's 2.5 cm to 500 km ruler is described.

Was on 32829 Greenwich Became the Standard in 1884, which is about fixing the Prime Meridian and says nothing about standard time. 32832 is where the chapter explains that using many local times would be inconvenient, so countries adopt a standard time, and its second LET'S EXPLORE asks for exactly this difference.

Was on 32828 Meridians and the Rotating Globe. The reason a globe represents the Earth better than a flat map - that the globe and the Earth have the same spherical shape - is stated in 32825, right after the orange-peel demonstration.
Was on 32828 Meridians and the Rotating Globe. Identifying the poles as the fixed points at the top and bottom when the globe is rotated is how 32827 opens, before building latitude from them.

Was on 32830 India's Own Prime Meridian at Ujjayini, which is the historical aside. Longitude being measured in degrees increasing westward or eastward from 0 to 180 is stated in 32829, along with the note that 180W and 180E are the same longitude.

Was on 32829 Greenwich Became the Standard in 1884. The worked example is verbatim in 32831 - if it is 12 noon at Greenwich it is 1 pm local time at 15E and 2 pm at 30E - which is the 15-degrees-to-the-hour rule the question applies.
Was on 32829 Greenwich Became the Standard in 1884. Indian Standard Time being 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time is stated in 32832, the standard-time concept.

Was on 32829 Greenwich Became the Standard in 1884. Why countries adopt a standard time - because it would not be convenient for a country to use many local times - is 32832's reasoning, which also covers the time zones that follow from it.
